topic: The Triangle of Power: A Unified Notation for Powers, Roots, and Logarithms
target_audience: High school students and math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Mathematical Fragmentations
sections.content: Introduce the problem: Traditional notation uses three completely different symbols (superscripts, radical signs, and 'log' abbreviations) to describe the same relationship between three numbers. Use an animation of a character, 'Leo the Architect', trying to build a bridge using three different manual types that don't match.
sections.example: Show 2³ = 8, ∛8 = 2, and log₂(8) = 3. Highlight how the numbers 2, 3, and 8 move positions confusingly in each format.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Three Roles
sections.content: Define the three components of any exponential relationship: The Base (the multiplier), the Exponent (the count), and the Result (the product). Use a 'Magnifying Glass' visual to identify these roles in a simple expression.
sections.example: In 2³ = 8, 2 is the 'Base' (The Root), 3 is the 'Exponent' (The Growth), and 8 is the 'Result' (The Value).

sections.title: Introducing the Triangle of Power
sections.content: Present a single geometric shape: An equilateral triangle. Map the roles to the vertices: Base at the bottom-left, Exponent at the top, and Result at the bottom-right. Explain that this single diagram replaces all three traditional notations.
sections.example: A glowing triangle appears. The number 2 sits at the bottom-left, 3 at the top, and 8 at the bottom-right. Lines connect them to show their interdependence.

sections.title: Operation 1: Calculating the Power
sections.content: When the bottom-left (Base) and top (Exponent) are known, we calculate the bottom-right (Result). In the triangle, this is visualized as the base 'climbing' to the exponent to produce the result.
sections.example: If the bottom-left is 5 and the top is 2, the bottom-right vertex pulses with a question mark until it transforms into 25 (5² = 25).

sections.title: Operation 2: Finding the Root
sections.content: When the top (Exponent) and bottom-right (Result) are known, we find the bottom-left (Base). This is the 'Root' operation. Visually, we are looking for the 'foundation' of the triangle.
sections.example: A triangle shows 3 at the top and 27 at the bottom-right. To find the bottom-left, we calculate the 3rd root of 27. The vertex fills in with 3.

sections.title: Operation 3: Solving the Logarithm
sections.content: When both bottom corners (Base and Result) are known, we find the top (Exponent). This is the 'Logarithm'. Visually, we are asking: 'To what height must the base be raised to reach this result?'
sections.example: A triangle shows 10 at the bottom-left and 1000 at the bottom-right. The top vertex is empty. The calculation reveals 3, because 10³ = 1000 (log₁₀ 1000 = 3).

sections.title: The Unified Summary
sections.content: Show all three operations happening on the same triangle simultaneously. Explain that by rotating our focus around the triangle, we transition between powers, roots, and logs without changing the underlying 'map' of the numbers.
sections.example: An animation shows Leo the Architect spinning a single triangle. As it rotates, it highlights different corners, showing how '2, 3, 8' always stay in their specific vertices regardless of which one is the 'unknown' x.
